lead: RSA is the public-key cipher you can run with paper and pencil. The sender raises the message to a public power modulo a large number n; the owner brings it back with a private exponent. It works because n is the product of two secret primes, and only the owner knows them. RSA protects TLS sessions, encrypted email, software updates and bank APIs, and its second job, signing, sits inside every certificate your phone checks.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for the trapdoor idea, and Unit 2 for Euler's theorem, the extended Euclidean algorithm and the Chinese remainder theorem.

blocks.text: RSA uses one public pair and one private number. The public pair (e, n) locks a message; the private number d unlocks it. Key generation builds all three from two secret primes.

items: Pick two large random primes p and q, each about half the target key size, and keep both secret.
Compute n = p×q. This is the modulus, and its bit length is the key size.
Compute φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1), the count of numbers from 1 to n−1 that are coprime to n. Keep it secret.
Choose the public exponent e with 1 < e < φ(n) and gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1. The usual value is 65537 = 2¹⁶ + 1: prime, only two 1-bits, so exponentiation is fast.
Compute d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n) with the extended Euclidean algorithm. This d is the private exponent.
Publish (e, n). Erase p, q and φ(n), or keep p and q safely for faster decryption by the Chinese remainder theorem.

blocks.where: e is the public exponent, d is the private exponent, and φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1) is Euler's totient of the modulus n. This congruence is the one working rule of the whole scheme.
m is the message written as an integer with 0 ≤ m < n, e and n are the public key, and c is the ciphertext integer.
d is the private exponent; the owner raises the ciphertext to d modulo n and gets the message back.

blocks.text: Practice replaces φ(n) by the smaller Carmichael value λ(n) = lcm(p−1, q−1). Any d with e·d ≡ 1 (mod λ(n)) also decrypts: λ(n) is a multiple of both p−1 and q−1, so e·d − 1 is a multiple of p−1 and of q−1; Fermat's little theorem then gives m^(e·d) ≡ m modulo p and modulo q, hence modulo n. Using λ(n) only enlarges the set of valid d compared with φ(n).

sections.h3: Why decryption gives back the message

blocks.text: Euler's theorem says m^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) whenever gcd(m, n) = 1. Key generation gave e·d = 1 + k·φ(n) for some whole number k.
c^d ≡ m^(e·d) = m·(m^φ(n))^k ≡ m·1ᵏ ≡ m (mod n)
blocks.where: c = mᵉ, so raising to d multiplies the exponent by d; the bracketed factor collapses to 1 by Euler's theorem.

blocks.text: So decryption costs one exponentiation and no searching. Now the leftover case gcd(m, n) ≠ 1. Then m is a multiple of p or of q, but not both, since m < n. Modulo p we get m ≡ 0, hence m^(e·d) ≡ 0 ≡ m. Modulo q Euler's theorem applies as usual. The Chinese remainder theorem glues the two answers into one value below n, so correctness holds for every m with 0 ≤ m < n.
The size limit is real: m must be smaller than n. Long data is never encrypted directly. RSA encrypts a short random key, and that key drives AES for the bulk data, as Unit 5 shows.

An attacker holds n, e and c and wants m. The best known attacks need the factorisation of n, and recovering d from (e, n) is provably as hard as factoring; no attack on RSA itself is known that beats factoring n. So RSA stands or falls with the difficulty of factoring n.

Current sizes: 2048 bits for new keys, 3072 bits for keys that must last for decades. A 2048-bit modulus is far beyond any published factorisation; the record sits near 250 decimal digits, about 829 bits.

items: Common modulus: two users share n with different e, and one message sent to both can be recovered without factoring.
Small e with small m: if mᵉ is below n, then c = mᵉ over ordinary integers, and an e-th root returns m.
Low private exponent: Wiener's attack recovers d when d is smaller than roughly n^(1/4), so d must be large.

Timing: decryption time follows the bits of d, so implementations use constant-time exponentiation (no data-dependent branches) and random blinding of the ciphertext to break the link between timing and d.
Chosen ciphertext: textbook RSA is multiplicative, so c₁·c₂ mod n decrypts to m₁·m₂ mod n, and an attacker can turn a decryption service into an oracle. Randomised padding such as OAEP blocks this.

blocks.text: Multiplicativity in one line: E(m₁)·E(m₂) = m₁ᵉ·m₂ᵉ = (m₁m₂)ᵉ = E(m₁m₂) mod n. The same m also always gives the same c. Textbook RSA is therefore malleable and deterministic, and no real system uses it bare.

figure.caption: The worked example end to end: p = 5 and q = 11 give n = 55 and φ(n) = 40, so e = 3 and d = 27; the message 9 encrypts to 14 and the owner brings it back to 9. The public pair (3, 55) goes out to everyone, while d = 27 stays with the owner and reappears only at the last step.

spec.title: RSA with p = 5, q = 11, e = 3, m = 9
spec.aria: The worked example runs top to bottom: secret primes 5 and 11 give n = 55 and φ(n) = 40, e = 3 is valid, d = 27 is computed and kept, the public pair (3, 55) encrypts m = 9 to c = 14, and d = 27 decrypts it back to 9.

examples.question: Let p = 5, q = 11, e = 3 and m = 9. Build the RSA key pair, encrypt m, and verify the decryption with the Chinese remainder theorem.
steps: n = p×q = 5×11 = 55. The modulus is 6 bits long, so this is a toy key.
gcd(3, 40) = 1, so e = 3 is a valid public exponent.
Find d: 3×27 = 81 = 2×40 + 1, so 3×27 ≡ 1 (mod 40) and d = 27. Here λ(n) = lcm(4, 10) = 20, so d = 7 works as well as 27; the example keeps 27 because it was computed mod φ(n).
Public key (e, n) = (3, 55); private key d = 27.
Decrypt by CRT. Mod 5: 14 ≡ 4, the order of 4 is 2, and 27 is odd, so 4²⁷ ≡ 4. Mod 11: 14 ≡ 3, the order of 3 is 5 because 3⁵ = 243 = 22×11 + 1, and 27 ≡ 2 (mod 5), so 3²⁷ ≡ 3² ≡ 9.
Combine: the value below 55 that is 4 mod 5 and 9 mod 11 is 9, and indeed 9 mod 5 = 4 and 9 mod 11 = 9.
examples.answer: The public key is (3, 55) and the private exponent is 27; the message m = 9 encrypts to c = 14 and decrypts back to m = 9.
examples.check:
from math import gcd

p, q, e, m = 5, 11, 3, 9
n = p * q
phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1)
assert gcd(e, phi) == 1
d = pow(e, -1, phi)
c = pow(m, e, n)
back = pow(c, d, n)
print(n)
print(phi)
print(d)
print(c)
print(back)

traps: Writing φ(n) = pq − 1. It is (p−1)(q−1): with p = 5, q = 11 the answer is 40, not 54.
Encrypting a message m ≥ n. Everything is mod n, so m = 60 with n = 55 quietly becomes 5 and the plaintext is lost. Split or pad so that m < n.
Believing d is unique. Every d ≡ e⁻¹ mod λ(n) decrypts; key files store the smallest positive one.
Calling textbook RSA secure. It is deterministic and multiplicative, so real systems add OAEP padding before the exponentiation.
Swapping the exponents. Encrypting with d instead of e is a signature, not encryption; see 4.8.

quiz.q: List the six steps of RSA key generation and say which values are public.
quiz.a: Pick secret primes p and q; set n = pq; set φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1); pick e with gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1; compute d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n); publish (e, n). Only e and n are public.

quiz.q: Why must φ(n), p and q stay secret when n itself is published?
quiz.a: Anyone holding φ(n) computes d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n) with the extended Euclidean algorithm and then decrypts everything. Holding p and q gives φ(n) at once, so the secret is really the factorisation of n.

quiz.q: Take p = 3, q = 7, e = 5 and m = 2. Find n, φ(n), d and the ciphertext c.
Using the modulus n = 55 and e = 3, show that E(4)·E(9) mod 55 equals E(36) mod 55.
quiz.a: E(4) = 4³ mod 55 = 64 mod 55 = 9. E(9) = 9³ mod 55 = 14. Product 9×14 = 126 = 2×55 + 16, so 16. E(36) = 36³ mod 55; 36 ≡ −19, and direct computation gives 16. The two agree, as multiplicativity predicts.

quiz.q: Why is a small public exponent dangerous when the message itself is small?
quiz.a: If mᵉ < n then no reduction happens modulo n, so c is the exact integer mᵉ. The attacker takes the ordinary e-th root and reads m. Padding makes m large and random so that mᵉ exceeds n.

quiz.q: Why does RSA need a randomised padding scheme such as OAEP before encryption?
quiz.a: Textbook RSA is deterministic and multiplicative, so a chosen-ciphertext attacker can multiply a target ciphertext by E(r) and ask for the decryption of the result. OAEP mixes in fresh randomness, breaks the algebraic relation and makes the scheme CCA-secure.

quiz.q: Why is e = 65537 the popular public exponent?
quiz.a: It is prime, so gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1 unless φ(n) is a multiple of 65537; it is 2¹⁶ + 1, so it has only two 1-bits and exponentiation needs very few multiplications; and it is large enough to avoid the small-exponent root attack on padded messages.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real deployments RSA is used mostly for signatures (RSASSA-PSS) and for wrapping a symmetric key; TLS 1.3 dropped RSA key exchange entirely in favour of ephemeral Diffie–Hellman. Shor's algorithm would factor n on a large quantum computer, which is why standards bodies are moving to lattice-based schemes such as ML-KEM. Side-channel hardening, constant-time modular exponentiation and blinding remain active engineering work. Search next for "RSA-OAEP", "RSASSA-PSS" and "post-quantum cryptography migration".
